tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

## plugin:desktop-commander:desktop-commander
Desktop Commander provides tools for working with the user's authorized device.
- Filesystem tools handle direct file and directory operations within configured access boundaries.
- Terminal process tools support shell commands, REPLs, and long-running processes. start_process creates a process session; interact_with_process sends input; read_process_output reads later output; force_terminate ends a session.
- Search tools are session-based. start_search creates a search session; get_more_search_results reads its results; stop_search ends it early.
- Absolute paths are generally the most reliable because relative paths depend on the active working directory.
- allowedDirectories and each tool's schema, annotations, and documented constraints define the operational boundaries.

Measured 2026-09-12 from a gap analysis of a Nate Herk / **Mark Kashef** video
("How to Actually Choose the Right AI Agent", 2026-09-11). Full note:
`~/SecondBrain/Inbox/2026-09-12-harness-over-model-mark-kashef.md`.
Same shape as the earlier audit in [[brain-audit-loop]] — that one scored the
**vault**, this one scores the **skill layer**.

## The measurement

| Metric | Count |
|---|---|
| Global skills in `~/.claude/skills/` | 160 (→ **117** after the Tier 1 archive, 2026-09-12) |
| Plugin skills exposed per session | ~37 (6 enabled, 18 disabled) |
| SKILL.md files in plugin cache | 606 — disabled plugins + old versions, NOT the load |
| Project-level skills anywhere in `~/DEV` | **0** |
| `.jsonl` sessions scanned | 414 |
| Distinct real skills **ever** invoked | **58** |
| Used 3+ times | 30 |
| Used exactly once | 19 |

Everything is global. That is the anti-pattern, not the achievement.

## The rule that fixes it — promotion

**Everything stays project-level until it earns global.** A skill lives in
`<project>/.claude/skills/` until it proves itself across 2+ projects, then it
gets promoted to `~/.claude/skills/`. Keeps the global load small and the blast
radius tight — so when something underperforms you can tell a *model* problem
from a *harness* problem from an *organisation* problem.

## The audit question

Not "how often did I run this skill?" but **"would the model do this fine without
the skill now?"** A skill is a crutch; as the brain gets smarter the crutch starts
to *limit* it. Seasonal skills (`forecast-capture`) and occasional ones
(`ingest-book`) are low-count by design — low usage alone is not a delete signal.

## Re-measure (BUILTIN filter is the whole trick)

Without the `BUILTIN` set you also count `/exit`, `/clear`, `/compact` and friends,
which inflates the total to 74 and buries the real skills.

```bash
python3 - <<'EOF'
import glob,re,collections
BUILTIN={'exit','clear','compact','rename','color','login','logout','plugin','doctor',
'help','model','config','resume','cost','status','init','agents','mcp','hooks','memory',
'review','vim','terminal-setup','install-github-app','add-dir','bug','release-notes',
'pr-comments','ide','permissions','statusline','output-style','todos','export',
'privacy-settings','upgrade','fast','artifacts','tasks','loop','context','usage','rewind',
'sandbox','feedback','worktrees','skills','reload-skills','reload-plugins','bashes',
'keybindings','theme'}
c=collections.Counter()
for f in glob.glob('/Users/kristinarash/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl',recursive=True):
    try:
        for line in open(f,encoding='utf-8',errors='ignore'):
            if 'Skill' not in line and 'command-name' not in line: continue
            for m in re.finditer(r'"name"\s*:\s*"Skill"\s*,\s*"input"\s*:\s*\{[^}]*?"skill"\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"', line):
                c[m.group(1)]+=1
            for m in re.finditer(r'<command-name>/([a-zA-Z0-9:_-]+)</command-name>', line):
                c[m.group(1)]+=1
    except Exception: pass
real={k:v for k,v in c.items() if k.split(':')[-1] not in BUILTIN and k not in BUILTIN}
print("distinct real skills ever invoked:",len(real))
print("used >=3 times:",len([k for k,v in real.items() if v>=3]))
print("used exactly once:",len([k for k,v in real.items() if v==1]))
for k,v in sorted(real.items(),key=lambda x:-x[1]): print(f"{v:5d}  {k}")
EOF
```

## Decision, 2026-09-12

**Do the skill audit BEFORE adopting Pi** (`pi.dev`) as an alternative harness. Superseded 2026-10-14: stay on Claude Code, no Pi (see [[agentic-operating-loop]]). The Pi facts below are kept as reference.
Rationale: the leverage is the bloat, not the harness. Auditing first means any
future harness move ports ~30 good skills instead of ~200 mixed ones.

Pi facts, verified from `pi.dev/docs/latest` 2026-09-12 — full note at
`~/SecondBrain/Inbox/2026-09-12-pi-harness-research.md`:

   Project trust only guards resource *loading*, not what the agent then does.

   said "weeks", that was wrong). Hooks here are already `.ts`; Pi's `tool_call` event

4. **Claude subscription through Pi bills per token as "extra usage", NOT against plan

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/plugins/cache/mattpocock/mattpocock-skills/1.3.2/skills/productivity/writing-for-agents

Reference for writing any document an agent consumes: a skill, an `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`, a doc reached by a pointer. The packaging differs; the writing does not: the same levers make each one predictable, since the agent takes the same _process_ every run rather than producing the same output.

When the document you're writing is a skill, read [`SKILL-MECHANICS.md`](SKILL-MECHANICS.md) for frontmatter, invocation choice, and router skills.

## Context pointers

A **context pointer** is a reference held in the agent's context that names some out-of-context material and encodes the condition for reaching it. A skill's description is one; a line in `AGENTS.md` naming a doc is the same object. The pointer's _wording_, not its target, decides when the agent reaches the material, and how reliably. A must-have target behind a weakly worded pointer is a variance bug: sharpen the wording first, and inline the material only if sharpening fails.

A pointer does two jobs: state what the material is, and list the **branches** that should trigger reaching it (a branch is a distinct case the document handles, so different runs take different paths through it). Every word of an always-loaded pointer costs on every turn, so it earns even harder pruning than the body:

- **Front-load the leading word**: the pointer is where it does its triggering work.
- **One trigger per branch.** Synonyms that rename a single branch are one branch written twice; collapse them and keep only genuinely distinct branches.
- **Cut identity the body already carries.**

## The two loads

Every document and pointer you add spends one of two budgets:

- **Context load** is the cost of always-loaded material on the agent's window: an `AGENTS.md` line, a skill description, anything sitting in context every turn, spending tokens and attention whether or not it fires.
- **Cognitive load** is the cost on the human: which documents exist and when to reach for each. The human is the index. Not a cost to minimise: it is the price of human agency; spend it where human judgement matters, remove it where it does not.

Material reached only through a pointer escapes context load at the price of the pointer's own line; material with no pointer at all rides entirely on cognitive load.

## Information hierarchy

A document is built from two content types: **steps** (the ordered actions the agent performs) and **reference** (definitions, rules, facts consulted on demand). The two mix freely: all steps (a recipe), all reference (a review's rules, this skill), or both. The core decision is where each piece sits on the **information hierarchy**, a ladder ranked by how immediately the agent needs the material:

1. **In-file step** is the primary tier: what the agent does, in order.
2. **In-file reference** is consulted on demand. Often a legitimately flat peer-set (every rule of a review on one rung), which is a fine arrangement, not a smell.
3. **Disclosed reference** is pushed out into a separate file, reached by a context pointer, loaded only when the pointer fires. Spans a sibling file in the same folder through fully external reference that lives anywhere and any document can point at.

Push too little down and the top bloats; push too much and you hide material the agent actually needs. That tension is the whole decision.

**Progressive disclosure** is the move down the ladder (out of the main file and behind a pointer) so the top stays legible. Not primarily a token optimisation: it is how the hierarchy is protected. Branching is the cleanest disclosure test: inline what every branch needs, and push behind a pointer what only some branches reach. When a document has steps, in-file reference that should be disclosed buries them and turns attending to them into a coin-flip: a variance lever, not just a legibility one.

**Co-location** is the within-file companion: where the ladder decides _how far down_ a piece sits, co-location decides _what sits beside it_ once there. Keep a concept's definition, rules, and caveats under one heading rather than scattered, so reading one part brings its neighbours with it. The test: the document should read like documentation written for the agent. Grouped material reads that way; scattered material does not. (Distinct from duplication: that repeats one meaning in two places; scattering fragments one meaning across many.)

**Sprawl** is the failure mode here: a document simply too long, even when every line is live and unique. Attention thins across the excess, and every extra line is one more to keep relevant. The cure is the ladder: disclose reference behind pointers, and split by branch or sequence so each path carries only what it needs.

## Steps and completion criteria

Every step ends on a **completion criterion**, the condition that tells the agent the work is done. Two properties make it a lever:

- **Clarity**: can the agent tell done from not-done? A vague bound ("understanding reached") invites **premature completion**: ending the step before it is genuinely done, attention slipping to _being done_. The visible steps still ahead (the **post-completion steps**) supply the pull; the criterion's clarity is the resistance. Defend in order: **sharpen the bound first** (local and cheap); only if it is irreducibly fuzzy _and_ you observe the rush, hide the later steps by splitting the sequence. Hiding only works across a real context boundary (a hand-off or a subagent dispatch; an inline call leaves the later steps in context and clears nothing).
- **Demand**: how much it requires. "Every modified model accounted for" forces thorough work where "produce a change list" does not. Demand drives **legwork** (the digging the agent does within the work, latent in the wording rather than written as its own step), and it is not step-bound: "every rule applied" binds a body of flat reference just as "every step done" binds a sequence, which is how an all-reference document still carries an exhaustiveness bar.

The strongest criteria are both checkable and exhaustive.

## When to split

Splitting one document into two spends one of the two loads, so split only when the cut earns it:

- **By sequence**: split a run of steps where the post-completion steps tempt the agent to rush the one in front of it. Keeping them out of view drives more legwork on the current task. Beware the reverse: merging sequences exposes each step's later steps to what follows, inviting premature completion.
- **By invocation**, skill-specific: see [`SKILL-MECHANICS.md`](SKILL-MECHANICS.md).

## Leading words

A **leading word** is a compact concept already living in the model's pretraining that the agent thinks with while running the document (_lesson_, _fog of war_, _tracer bullets_). Repeated as a token, never as a sentence, it accumulates a distributed definition and anchors a whole region of behaviour in the fewest tokens, by recruiting priors the model already holds. Coining your own works if you define it clearly, but a made-up word recruits no priors: you pay in definition tokens what a pretrained word gives free; reach for an existing word first.

It anchors twice. In the body, _execution_: the agent reaches for the same behaviour every time the word appears, and inside flat reference it focuses attention on a class of thing to look for. In a pointer, _invocation_: when the same word lives in your prompts, your docs, and your codebase, the agent links that shared language to the material and reaches it more reliably.

Hunt for opportunities to refactor with leading words. A triad spelled out at three sites, a pointer spending a sentence to gesture at one idea. Each is a passage begging to collapse into a single token:

- "fast, deterministic, low-overhead" → _tight_ (a _tight_ loop).
- "a loop you believe in" → _red_, turning a fuzzy gate into a binary observable state (the loop goes _red_ on the bug, or it doesn't).

You win twice: fewer tokens, and a sharper hook for the agent to hang its thinking on. Assume every document is carrying restatements that leading words retire. Go find them.

**Negation** is the failure mode beside this lever: steering by prohibition drags the forbidden behaviour into context and makes it _more_ available, not less. _Don't think of an elephant_, and the elephant is all there is; the negation is a weak modifier the strongly-activated concept overruns, so the ban half-reads as an instruction to do the thing. Prompt the **positive**: state the target behaviour ("write one-line comments") so the banned one is never spoken. A prohibition earns its place only as a hard guardrail you cannot phrase positively; even then, pair it with the positive target so attention lands on what to do.

## Pruning

- Keep each meaning in a **single source of truth**: one authoritative place, so changing the behaviour is a one-place edit. **Duplication** (the same meaning in more than one place) costs maintenance and tokens, and inflates a meaning's prominence on the ladder past its real rank. (The accidental inverse of a leading word, which repeats a token on purpose, never the meaning.)
- The **environment** is a source of truth too (`package.json` scripts, config files, the directory layout, `--help` output), and a document that restates it is a **cache**: a copy of a lookup, earning its load only when the lookup is expensive. Cache what the agent cannot find by looking: the unwritten convention, the reason behind a choice, the gotcha no config confesses. Leave the one-file, one-command lookups to the environment, where they cannot go stale.
- Check every line for **relevance**: does it still bear on what the document does? A line loses relevance by never bearing on the task (mere exposition, or a branch that should be disclosed) or by going stale as the behaviour or world it describes changes. Shorter documents are easier to keep relevant. Without a pruning discipline the default fate is **sediment**: stale layers that settle because adding feels safe and removing feels risky, until you must core down through them to find what is still live.
- Hunt **no-ops** sentence by sentence: an instruction the model already obeys by default pays load to say nothing. The test (does it change behaviour versus the default?) is model-relative, not reader-relative: two people disagreeing about a no-op disagree about the default, and settle it by running the document, not by debate. When a sentence fails, delete the whole sentence rather than trim words from it. The test also grades leading words: a word too weak to beat the default (_be thorough_ when the agent is already thorough-ish) is a no-op, and the fix is a stronger word (_relentless_), not a different technique.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

## plugin:desktop-commander:desktop-commander
Desktop Commander provides tools for working with the user's authorized device.
- Filesystem tools handle direct file and directory operations within configured access boundaries.
- Terminal process tools support shell commands, REPLs, and long-running processes. start_process creates a process session; interact_with_process sends input; read_process_output reads later output; force_terminate ends a session.
- Search tools are session-based. start_search creates a search session; get_more_search_results reads its results; stop_search ends it early.
- Absolute paths are generally the most reliable because relative paths depend on the active working directory.
- allowedDirectories and each tool's schema, annotations, and documented constraints define the operational boundaries.

1	---
2	name: dev-sync
3	description: >-
4	  Bring this machine into line with GitHub and load back the context that came with it:
5	  locate DEV automatically, pull config and skills, inventory every project, commit and
6	  push local work, pull the other machine's work, clone what is missing, report
7	  conflicts, then read the repo's STATUS and latest handoff and report where the last
8	  session left off. Use when Eric switches machines, sits down to start work, says 'sync
9	  DEV', asks whether everything is pushed, or asks where he left off. Do not use when
10	  Eric says '/startup' or 'good morning' (use startup, which runs this sync) or to
11	  scaffold a new repo (use new-project).
12	---
13	
14	# DEV sync
15	
16	Eric works on a Mac and a Windows laptop. GitHub (`erash11`, all private) is the transport. This skill makes the current machine match GitHub without losing anything on either side. It is the first thing to run when sitting down at a machine.
17	
18	## Step 0: find DEV (never depend on cwd)
19	
20	Eric may run this from anywhere. Detect the machine and go to its DEV root:
21	
22	- macOS (`uname` = Darwin): `~/DEV`
23	- Windows (PowerShell, or `$OS` = Windows_NT): `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV`
24	
25	If that folder does not exist, stop and say so. Do not guess another location. Print the root you chose on the first line of output.
26	
27	## Step 1: config and skills
28	
29	These are separate repos and the other machine may have changed them:
30	
31	1. `~/.claude` (repo `dotclaude`): `git pull`. If `~/.claude/machine.md` is missing, copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` for this OS. Then sync the mods: `bash ~/.claude/mods/mods-sync.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\mods\mods-sync.ps1` (Windows). The folder is the list; put its one line (`mods: N loaded, N disabled, N invalid`) in the report and name any invalid mod. Then apply the 7-day rule: `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py seven-day --apply` (`portfolio_json` in `_shared/config.<platform>.json`). It pauses any project started more than 7 days ago with no receiver and no step 1 done, and prints one line plus each project paused or on the clock; put that in the report.
32	2. `~/.claude/skills` (repo `claude-skills`): `git pull`, then run `sync-to-codex.sh` (Mac) or `sync-to-codex.ps1` (Windows) so Codex sees the shared skills.
33	3. `~/.claude/global-memory` (repo `claude-global-memory`): `git pull`. **This is the only thing that carries memory between the two machines.** USER.md and MEMORY.md live here, with the handoff history (new handoffs go to `<repo>/docs/handoffs/` or `~/DEV/docs/handoffs/`). `daily-backup` pushes this repo nightly, but nothing pulled it at the start of a session until this step existed, so a same-day handoff (worked on the Mac after lunch, picked up on Windows that evening) arrived with stale memory. Pull it before anything else reads it. If the pull brings in commits, say how many and name the newest, so it is visible that memory moved.
34	
35	If any of the three has local uncommitted changes, commit them first with `<machine> snapshot before sync`, then pull, then push.
36	
37	4. **Mirror project memory across the two slugs.** Tier A memory is keyed by a slug built from the absolute path, so every project has a Mac folder (`-Users-kristinarash-DEV-X`) and a Windows folder (`C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-X`) under `~/.claude/projects/`. dotclaude carries both to both machines, but each machine auto-loads only its own. Before this step existed, 43 memories written on the Mac never loaded on Windows (found 2026-09-24). After the pulls above, run:
38	
39	   - Mac: `python3 ~/.claude/skills/dev-sync/mirror_memory.py`
40	   - Windows: `python $HOME\.claude\skills\dev-sync\mirror_memory.py`
41	
42	   It copies files one side lacks, lets the newer version win when both have one (frontmatter `modified:`, else last commit), merges `MEMORY.md` indexes line by line, creates the twin folder when a project has memory on only one machine, and never deletes. The older side of any replaced file stays in dotclaude history. Put its summary line in the Step 4 report. If it wrote anything, commit `~/.claude` with `<machine> memory mirror` and push, so the other machine gets the result on its next sync.
43	
44	   Mirroring is a union: a memory deleted on one machine comes back from the other. To retire a memory for good, delete it from both slug folders in the same commit.
45	
46	Merge note for `global-memory`: `transcripts/.errors.log` and `MEMORY.md` are both append-heavy and both machines write them. On conflict, keep both sides' content rather than choosing one — these are logs, not settings, and a dropped line is a lost memory.
47	
48	## Step 2: inventory (always show before changing anything)
49	
50	Walk `DEV/*`, `DEV/Football/*`, and `DEV/SpecialRequests/*`. Skip `.claude`, `_tools`, `_DRIVE` (a link to the Google Drive primary storage drive, not a project; never init it, never walk into it), `token-dashboard` (someone else's remote), and any folder ending in `_OLD_merged*`. For each folder report one of:
51	
52	- **repo + erash11 remote**: uncommitted count, unpushed count
53	- **repo, no remote**: needs `gh repo create`
54	- **not a repo**: needs init + create (use the `new-project` skill's file set)
55	
56	Then `gh repo list erash11 --limit 300 --no-archived --json name` and list repos with no local folder. Skip: `dotclaude` (that is `~/.claude`), `SecondBrain`, `claude-skills`, `claude-memory-compiler`, `DEV`, `DexaProject`.
57	
58	Eric pre-approves these operations; the inventory is for visibility, not a pause for approval, unless something looks wrong (a repo with hundreds of uncommitted files, a large file about to be added).
59	
60	**Group the report by activity, not alphabetically.** Run `~/.claude/scripts/dev-activity.sh` (Mac) or `dev-activity.ps1` (Windows), which ranks repos by distinct commit days over 90 days. List the active ones individually and collapse the rest to a count: "118 dormant repos: all clean" is the useful line, not 118 names. About 14 repos are genuinely worked at any time; the rest are archives that happen to live in the same folder.
61	
62	Rank by **commit days, not recency**. On 2026-09-09 a bulk migration gave 43 repos one commit each, after which every one of them looked active by any recency measure. Days-worked is not fooled by that, because a migration touches a repo once.
63	
64	Nothing is archived or moved on the strength of this. Sorting is a reporting concern. Moving a dormant repo into an archive folder breaks two things: KeystoneOS `projects.json`, `memory-sources.json`, `memory-index-paths.json` and `discovery-roots.json` hold DEV paths; and Tier A project memory is keyed by a slug derived from the absolute path, so moving a repo orphans its memory. (A third is fixed: since 2026-10-24 `harvest-dev-docs` also mirrors `_ARCHIVE/*/docs` into `dev-docs/_ARCHIVE/`, so archived repos stay searchable.) Checked 2026-09-12. Do not revive the archive idea without fixing both first.
65	
66	## Step 3: apply, per repo
67	
68	1. If uncommitted: put any untracked file over 95 MB and any `.env` into `.gitignore`, then `git add -A && git commit -m "<machine> snapshot before sync"`.
69	2. `git fetch origin` then `git merge --no-edit origin/<branch>`.
70	3. On conflict: keep this machine's version, save the remote version beside it as `<file>.from-mac` or `<file>.from-windows` (whichever the other machine is), stage both, commit. Never discard either side. `.DS_Store` conflicts: just delete the file.
71	
72	   Save the remote side by **moving the file, never by redirecting stdout**. A
73	   redirect re-encodes the bytes; on Windows that silently mangles every
74	   non-ASCII character (an em-dash becomes `ΓÇö`) and adds a UTF-8 BOM, so the
75	   saved copy is corrupt and every later diff shows a phantom first-line change.
76	
77	   - PowerShell: `git checkout --theirs -- <f>; Move-Item <f> <f>.from-mac; git checkout --ours -- <f>`
78	   - bash: `git checkout --theirs -- <f> && mv <f> <f>.from-mac && git checkout --ours -- <f>`
79	
80	   Never run `git add -A` while `.git/MERGE_HEAD` exists — it stages the
81	   conflict markers themselves and commits a broken file. Stage only the named
82	   paths you just resolved.
83	4. `git push`.
84	5. Missing locally: `gh repo clone erash11/<name> DEV/<name>`.
85	6. No remote: `gh repo create erash11/<name> --private --source=. --push`.
86	
87	Windows note: line-ending noise (`LF will be replaced by CRLF`) is normal. If a merge refuses to start because of phantom modifications, run `git add --renormalize .` and commit before merging.
88	
89	Stale-lock note: if a commit or push fails with `cannot lock ref 'HEAD'`, check
90	`pgrep -fl git` (or `Get-Process git`) first. If no git is running and the
91	`.git/*.lock` file is zero bytes and older than the session, it is stale from an
92	interrupted run. Move it aside — do not delete it — then retry.
93	
94	## Step 4: verify and report
95	
96	Re-walk every repo. Report: DEV root used, config and skills pulled (yes/no), the memory-mirror summary line, repos checked, pulled, cloned, created, and any folder still dirty or unpushed. List every `.from-*` file created so Eric can reconcile them. Finish with one line: clean or not.
97	
98	## Step 4b: start the project board
99	
100	The live board (`project-triage/board.py`, PM system design Decision 10) writes `portfolio.json`, so it may only start on a registry that has the other machine's edits. Start it only when project-triage came through Step 3 clean: pulled, no `.git/MERGE_HEAD`, no `portfolio.json.from-*` file. Then run, from the folder holding `portfolio_json`:
101	
102	- Windows: `python board.py --background`
103	- Mac: `python3 board.py --background`
104	
105	It reuses a board already running on this machine or starts one tied to this session, opens the page, and prints `board started at <url>` or `board already running at <url>`; put that line in the report. If project-triage did not come through clean, do not start it; report `board: not started, project-triage pull unresolved` and name the conflict. Eric's `pm` (shell) and `/pm` (Claude Code) run the same command later in the day.
106	
107	## Step 5: pick up where the other machine left off
108	
109	Syncing git state is only half the job. The other half is loading the context that came with it, and nothing else does this — the SessionStart hook injects global memory, but project state lives in the repo, and Tier A project memory only crosses machines through the Step 1 mirror. This step is the only place that repo context gets read back in.
110	
111	Do this for the repo Eric names, or the one he is in. If he has not named one, pick from the ACTIVE list in Step 2, not from all 132: take the active repo with the most recent commit and say which you chose. ---
name: dev-sync
description: >-
  Bring this machine into line with GitHub and load back the context that came with it:
  locate DEV automatically, pull config and skills, inventory every project, commit and
  push local work, pull the other machine's work, clone what is missing, report
  conflicts, then read the repo's STATUS and latest handoff and report where the last
  session left off. Use when Eric switches machines, sits down to start work, says 'sync
  DEV', asks whether everything is pushed, or asks where he left off. Do not use when
  Eric says '/startup' or 'good morning' (use startup, which runs this sync) or to
  scaffold a new repo (use new-project).
---

# DEV sync

Eric works on a Mac and a Windows laptop. GitHub (`erash11`, all private) is the transport. This skill makes the current machine match GitHub without losing anything on either side. It is the first thing to run when sitting down at a machine.

## Step 0: find DEV (never depend on cwd)

Eric may run this from anywhere. Detect the machine and go to its DEV root:

- macOS (`uname` = Darwin): `~/DEV`
- Windows (PowerShell, or `$OS` = Windows_NT): `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV`

If that folder does not exist, stop and say so. Do not guess another location. Print the root you chose on the first line of output.

## Step 1: config and skills

These are separate repos and the other machine may have changed them:

1. `~/.claude` (repo `dotclaude`): `git pull`. If `~/.claude/machine.md` is missing, copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` for this OS. Then sync the mods: `bash ~/.claude/mods/mods-sync.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\mods\mods-sync.ps1` (Windows). The folder is the list; put its one line (`mods: N loaded, N disabled, N invalid`) in the report and name any invalid mod. Then apply the 7-day rule: `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py seven-day --apply` (`portfolio_json` in `_shared/config.<platform>.json`). It pauses any project started more than 7 days ago with no receiver and no step 1 done, and prints one line plus each project paused or on the clock; put that in the report.
2. `~/.claude/skills` (repo `claude-skills`): `git pull`, then run `sync-to-codex.sh` (Mac) or `sync-to-codex.ps1` (Windows) so Codex sees the shared skills.
3. `~/.claude/global-memory` (repo `claude-global-memory`): `git pull`. **This is the only thing that carries memory between the two machines.** USER.md and MEMORY.md live here, with the handoff history (new handoffs go to `<repo>/docs/handoffs/` or `~/DEV/docs/handoffs/`). `daily-backup` pushes this repo nightly, but nothing pulled it at the start of a session until this step existed, so a same-day handoff (worked on the Mac after lunch, picked up on Windows that evening) arrived with stale memory. Pull it before anything else reads it. If the pull brings in commits, say how many and name the newest, so it is visible that memory moved.

If any of the three has local uncommitted changes, commit them first with `<machine> snapshot before sync`, then pull, then push.

4. **Mirror project memory across the two slugs.** Tier A memory is keyed by a slug built from the absolute path, so every project has a Mac folder (`-Users-kristinarash-DEV-X`) and a Windows folder (`C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-X`) under `~/.claude/projects/`. dotclaude carries both to both machines, but each machine auto-loads only its own. Before this step existed, 43 memories written on the Mac never loaded on Windows (found 2026-09-24). After the pulls above, run:

   - Mac: `python3 ~/.claude/skills/dev-sync/mirror_memory.py`
   - Windows: `python $HOME\.claude\skills\dev-sync\mirror_memory.py`

   It copies files one side lacks, lets the newer version win when both have one (frontmatter `modified:`, else last commit), merges `MEMORY.md` indexes line by line, creates the twin folder when a project has memory on only one machine, and never deletes. The older side of any replaced file stays in dotclaude history. Put its summary line in the Step 4 report. If it wrote anything, commit `~/.claude` with `<machine> memory mirror` and push, so the other machine gets the result on its next sync.

   Mirroring is a union: a memory deleted on one machine comes back from the other. To retire a memory for good, delete it from both slug folders in the same commit.

Merge note for `global-memory`: `transcripts/.errors.log` and `MEMORY.md` are both append-heavy and both machines write them. On conflict, keep both sides' content rather than choosing one — these are logs, not settings, and a dropped line is a lost memory.

## Step 2: inventory (always show before changing anything)

Walk `DEV/*`, `DEV/Football/*`, and `DEV/SpecialRequests/*`. Skip `.claude`, `_tools`, `_DRIVE` (a link to the Google Drive primary storage drive, not a project; never init it, never walk into it), `token-dashboard` (someone else's remote), and any folder ending in `_OLD_merged*`. For each folder report one of:

- **repo + erash11 remote**: uncommitted count, unpushed count
- **repo, no remote**: needs `gh repo create`
- **not a repo**: needs init + create (use the `new-project` skill's file set)

Then `gh repo list erash11 --limit 300 --no-archived --json name` and list repos with no local folder. Skip: `dotclaude` (that is `~/.claude`), `SecondBrain`, `claude-skills`, `claude-memory-compiler`, `DEV`, `DexaProject`.

Eric pre-approves these operations; the inventory is for visibility, not a pause for approval, unless something looks wrong (a repo with hundreds of uncommitted files, a large file about to be added).

**Group the report by activity, not alphabetically.** Run `~/.claude/scripts/dev-activity.sh` (Mac) or `dev-activity.ps1` (Windows), which ranks repos by distinct commit days over 90 days. List the active ones individually and collapse the rest to a count: "118 dormant repos: all clean" is the useful line, not 118 names. About 14 repos are genuinely worked at any time; the rest are archives that happen to live in the same folder.

Rank by **commit days, not recency**. On 2026-09-09 a bulk migration gave 43 repos one commit each, after which every one of them looked active by any recency measure. Days-worked is not fooled by that, because a migration touches a repo once.

Nothing is archived or moved on the strength of this. Sorting is a reporting concern. Moving a dormant repo into an archive folder breaks two things: KeystoneOS `projects.json`, `memory-sources.json`, `memory-index-paths.json` and `discovery-roots.json` hold DEV paths; and Tier A project memory is keyed by a slug derived from the absolute path, so moving a repo orphans its memory. (A third is fixed: since 2026-10-24 `harvest-dev-docs` also mirrors `_ARCHIVE/*/docs` into `dev-docs/_ARCHIVE/`, so archived repos stay searchable.) Checked 2026-09-12. Do not revive the archive idea without fixing both first.

## Step 3: apply, per repo

1. If uncommitted: put any untracked file over 95 MB and any `.env` into `.gitignore`, then `git add -A && git commit -m "<machine> snapshot before sync"`.
2. `git fetch origin` then `git merge --no-edit origin/<branch>`.
3. On conflict: keep this machine's version, save the remote version beside it as `<file>.from-mac` or `<file>.from-windows` (whichever the other machine is), stage both, commit. Never discard either side. `.DS_Store` conflicts: just delete the file.

   Save the remote side by **moving the file, never by redirecting stdout**. A
   redirect re-encodes the bytes; on Windows that silently mangles every
   non-ASCII character (an em-dash becomes `ΓÇö`) and adds a UTF-8 BOM, so the
   saved copy is corrupt and every later diff shows a phantom first-line change.

   - PowerShell: `git checkout --theirs -- <f>; Move-Item <f> <f>.from-mac; git checkout --ours -- <f>`
   - bash: `git checkout --theirs -- <f> && mv <f> <f>.from-mac && git checkout --ours -- <f>`

   Never run `git add -A` while `.git/MERGE_HEAD` exists — it stages the
   conflict markers themselves and commits a broken file. Stage only the named
   paths you just resolved.
4. `git push`.
5. Missing locally: `gh repo clone erash11/<name> DEV/<name>`.
6. No remote: `gh repo create erash11/<name> --private --source=. --push`.

Windows note: line-ending noise (`LF will be replaced by CRLF`) is normal. If a merge refuses to start because of phantom modifications, run `git add --renormalize .` and commit before merging.

Stale-lock note: if a commit or push fails with `cannot lock ref 'HEAD'`, check
`pgrep -fl git` (or `Get-Process git`) first. If no git is running and the
`.git/*.lock` file is zero bytes and older than the session, it is stale from an
interrupted run. Move it aside — do not delete it — then retry.

## Step 4: verify and report

Re-walk every repo. Report: DEV root used, config and skills pulled (yes/no), the memory-mirror summary line, repos checked, pulled, cloned, created, and any folder still dirty or unpushed. List every `.from-*` file created so Eric can reconcile them. Finish with one line: clean or not.

## Step 4b: start the project board

The live board (`project-triage/board.py`, PM system design Decision 10) writes `portfolio.json`, so it may only start on a registry that has the other machine's edits. Start it only when project-triage came through Step 3 clean: pulled, no `.git/MERGE_HEAD`, no `portfolio.json.from-*` file. Then run, from the folder holding `portfolio_json`:

- Windows: `python board.py --background`
- Mac: `python3 board.py --background`

It reuses a board already running on this machine or starts one tied to this session, opens the page, and prints `board started at <url>` or `board already running at <url>`; put that line in the report. If project-triage did not come through clean, do not start it; report `board: not started, project-triage pull unresolved` and name the conflict. Eric's `pm` (shell) and `/pm` (Claude Code) run the same command later in the day.

## Step 5: pick up where the other machine left off

Syncing git state is only half the job. The other half is loading the context that came with it, and nothing else does this — the SessionStart hook injects global memory, but project state lives in the repo, and Tier A project memory only crosses machines through the Step 1 mirror. This step is the only place that repo context gets read back in.

Do this for the repo Eric names, or the one he is in. If he has not named one, pick from the ACTIVE list in Step 2, not from all 132: take the active repo with the most recent commit and say which you chose. A dormant repo receiving one migration commit must never win this, which is exactly what picking by recency across everything would do.

1. Read `<repo>/AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md` if there is no AGENTS.md).
2. Read `<repo>/docs/STATUS.md`.
3. Read the newest file in `<repo>/docs/handoffs/`, if the folder exists and its newest file is within about two weeks.
4. If `docs/STATUS.md` does not exist in a repo that has real work in it, say so — that repo is invisible to the other machine and closeout should have created it.
5. Run `python ~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py --decisions --days 3`. It lists every open item under `## Open questions` in each repo whose STATUS changed in the window, plus the dated handoffs written in it. Steps 1–4 cover one repo; this is what keeps a multi-repo day from shrinking to that one repo's "Blocked on" line. Three days covers a weekend; use `--days 7` after a longer gap.

Then report before doing any work: six lines or fewer for the picked repo, then the decisions block:

```
Picking up: <repo>
Last session: <date>, <mac|windows>
Where things stand: <two lines from STATUS.md Current state>
Blocked on: <open questions, or "nothing">
Next: <top one or two from STATUS.md Next>

Decisions waiting on you (<N> in <M> repos):
- <repo>: <question, one line>
...
Handoffs since <date>: <repo/file>, ...
```

List the decisions newest repo first, one line each, trimmed to the question itself. If an item is only a pointer ("See PLAN.md …"), open the file it names and list the actual questions, then flag that repo's STATUS for a fix at the next closeout. If there are more than about twelve, show those from the last day in full and name the rest by repo with a count.

Stop there and wait for Eric to confirm or redirect. Do not start the next task off the back of STATUS.md on your own — it records where work stopped, not what he wants to do this morning.

## Do not

- Do not `rm` anything. Move to a `_to_delete` or `_OLD_*` folder if something must get out of the way.
- Do not rebase or force-push.
- Do not push DexaProject or any repo whose CLAUDE.md says its data must stay local.

1	---

3	description: >-

10	# Closeout
11	
12	One command for the end-of-day sequence: loose ends → memory → STATUS and handoff → commit and push → one verdict.
13	
14	Run every step without pausing: invoking closeout authorizes the whole sequence. Commit and push is
15	standing-authorized for every DEV repo (each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine ends with it, and
16	unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other). On Windows or in Cowork,

18

21	A repo whose `CLAUDE.md` says its data stays local (DexaProject is the precedent) is committed,
22	not pushed, and listed.
23	
24	**Clear to sign off when** the closing `where-was-i.py --sweep` (step 4) shows no `ACTION` line
25	except repos listed under "Still open" with their reason, no background job is still writing,
26	`.errors.log` is empty or its entries are reported, and every repo touched today has a STATUS entry
27	dated today with a concrete first `## Next` item, and every `card-check` gap is fixed. Questions
28	only Eric can answer (a receiver nobody named, a decision recorded under `## Open questions`) do
29	not block: `/startup` shows them tomorrow; list them under "Still open" and say "Clear to sign off".
30	Anything short of that: "Not clear", naming the one thing blocking.
31	
32	If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and
33	note it. A risky fix goes under "Still open".
34	
35	## Step 1 — Sweep
36	
37	- **Repo sweep:** `python3 ~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py --sweep` (~4 s). It checks every git
38	  repo under `DEV/` (two levels) and the three config repos, and prints one line per repo needing
39	  attention; exit 1 means at least one `ACTION`. Another session, harness or machine may have left
40	  that work; name each such repo in the report. Flags:
41	  - `DIRTY`, `UNPUSHED`, `NO-UPSTREAM`, `BRANCH-AHEAD:<b>`, `BRANCH-UNPUSHED:<b>` (a local branch
42	    holding commits on no remote), `WORKTREE-DIRTY:<path>`: work not on GitHub. Step 4 pushes it.
43	  - `NOT-A-REPO`: a `.git` folder git cannot use, so the folder's work is tracked nowhere. List it;
44	    repair is project work, not closeout. It blocks only if this session wrote files there.
45	  - Info, never blocking: `STASH:<n>` (list it; leave the stash alone), `NO-REMOTE`, `DETACHED`
46	    (a pinned checkout), `LIVE` (session files the hooks rewrite every turn; the daily backup
47	    pushes them).
48	- **Background jobs** still running (shells, agents, workflows): wait for each to finish, or name
49	  it as the blocker. A job that writes after the push leaves work unpushed.
50	- **Registry drift:** `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py crosswalk` (`portfolio_json` is
51	  in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.macos.json`). It only reports. List every item under "Still
52	  open", any folder created this session first (a project started without a row). Fixing waits
53	  for a project session. `drive_unreachable` means the Drive checks never ran: say so.
54	- **7-day rule:** `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py seven-day --apply`. Name every
55	  project it paused, and any on its last two days, under "Still open" with what it needs (a
56	  receiver, a first step).
57	- Unfinished tasks from this session (TaskList), and anything promised to Eric this session and
58	  not delivered.
59	
60	## Step 2 — Memory
61	
62	Memory capture failing silently is Eric's top recurring worry; this step runs every time.
63	
64	- **`~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log`:** surface every entry, fix the hook issue if
65	  obvious, then archive and clear it as in claude-stack-doctor's `FIXES.md` → Memory pipeline
66	  (append to `.errors-ledger.log`, then `cp /dev/null`). The file is tracked in `global-memory`,
67	  so this happens before step 4's push.
68	- **Today's transcript** `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` exists and changed within
69	  the last few hours.
70	- **New durable decision or active thread:** update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md`
71	  (2,500-char cap; consolidate first) or write a Tier A memory with the `memory-write` skill.
72	- **Tier A stays on this machine** (its slug is built from the absolute path, which differs per
73	  machine). Every durable, project-scoped Tier A fact written today also goes into the repo:
74	  `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reason, the dated
75	  handoff for detail.
76	
77	## Step 3 — STATUS, handoff, cards
78	
79	**Handoff**, when real work happened (not just Q&A): `<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md`;
80	workspace or system work with no single repo goes to `~/DEV/docs/handoffs/`
81	(`~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` is read-only history). Plain markdown that Codex,
82	Antigravity or a fresh Claude session can resume from:
83	- what was worked on and why
84	- decisions made, with the reasoning that would be lost
85	- exact paths of every file created or modified
86	- next actions, most important first
87	- anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)
88	
89	**`docs/STATUS.md`, in every repo touched, every time.** The next session reads it first, on
90	either machine, in any harness. Rewrite these sections in place, short:
91	- `## Current state`: two to five lines on where things stand today.
92	- `## Next`: most important first. Item 1 is one concrete action (a command to run or a file to
93	  open); `~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py` shows it to Eric the next morning.
94	- `## Open questions`: each decision waiting on Eric as its own top-level bullet, the question and
95	  enough context to answer it without opening another file. `/startup` lists this section across
96	  repos, so write the question itself, never a pointer. Mark answered items `ANSWERED <date>: …`
97	  or strike them (`~~…~~`). Leave the section empty when nothing waits.
98	- `## Gotchas`: anything that will bite the next session.
99	
100	Over 20 KB, or more than 15 dated entries under `## Current state`: first move entries older than
101	14 days and finished `## Next` items, verbatim, to the end of
102	`docs/handoffs/STATUS-archive-<YYYY>-Q<n>.md`. The archive is a search root; entries move, they
103	are never deleted.
104	
105	Then:
106	1. `python ~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py --decisions --days 1` prints what tomorrow's
107	   `/startup` shows as "Decisions waiting on you". Every decision left open today appears there as
108	   a readable question; fix the repo's `## Open questions` until it does.
109	2. `python <dir of portfolio_json>/landed.py scan --days 1` (~1 min), then
110	   `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py card-check`. Fix every gap with
111	   [`CARDS.md`](CARDS.md), then re-run `card-check`.
112	3. `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh`: copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into
113	   `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/` (gitignored, indexed by memsearch). One line of output.
114	4. **Deliverables:** a finished file made for someone else today (PDF, deck, report, sheet) gets a
115	   copy at `~/DEV/_DRIVE/03_REPORTS/YYYY-MM-DD_<Sport>_<Topic>_<Audience>.<ext>`. The repo keeps
116	   the source.
117	
118	## Step 4 — Commit and push
119	
120	- **Registry edits first, alone.** In project-triage, if `git status --porcelain portfolio.json`
121	  shows a change, commit that file alone as `data: board edits <YYYY-MM-DD>`. The board's "N
122	  unpushed registry edits" counts these; folded into another commit, they become a JSON merge
123	  conflict when the other machine edits too.
124	- **Before staging,** read the files about to be added (`git status --porcelain`). Anything the
125	  `BLOCKED` list in `~/.claude/hooks/session-autopush.js` names (`.env`, keys, credentials,
126	  secrets, token files, databases, DEXA) or over 50 MB stays out: add it to `.gitignore`, or leave
127	  it unstaged and list it. Health data never reaches GitHub.
128	- Every repo in scope: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase`, push. On
129	  a merge conflict follow `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (the one home for conflict steps), push, and list the
130	  file under "Still open". A side branch the sweep flagged: `git push -u origin <branch>`.
131	- `~/.claude/mods` changed this session: `bash ~/.claude/mods/mods-sync.sh`; list any invalid mod.
132	- **`global-memory` is pushed every time,** even on a light session: it is the only repo that
133	  carries memory to the other machine, and the nightly backup is too late for a same-day switch.
134	- Nothing to commit: one line, move on.
135	- **Prove it:** re-run `python3 ~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py --sweep`. Every `ACTION` line left
136	  is either fixed now or goes under "Still open" with its reason. A push that hangs is usually a
137	  credential prompt: look for `git credential-osxkeychain get` in `ps`; fix and retry once, as
138	  `~/.claude/projects/-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory/project_brew-git-keychain-hang.md` says.
139	  Still hanging: "Not clear", that repo is the blocker.
140	
141	## Step 5 — Verdict
142	
143	`python <dir of portfolio_json>/landed.py show --days 1` lists every file that landed today (git in
144	every DEV repo, file times on Drive and in the vault), so the report names every created or
145	modified file with its full path. The ledger lives in `~/.claude/global-memory/landed/` and was
146	pushed in step 4.
147	
148	```
149	## Closeout — <date>
150	
151	**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
152	**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
153	**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what> / skipped: <what> (Cowork)
154	**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
155	**Registry drift:** <N items, or "none">
156	**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">
157	
158	Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
159	
160	**Landed:** <landed.py show output, grouped by project>
161	**Cards:** <card-check output after the step 3 fixes>
162	```
163	
164	The block above the verdict line fits on one screen: Eric is leaving. Landed and Cards come last
165	because the next session picks up from them; trim both to projects with work today, keeping every
166	card that still has a gap.

**Scope.** Every DEV repo with uncommitted or unpushed work (touched this session or not), plus
`~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory`.
A repo whose `CLAUDE.md` says its data stays local (DexaProject is the precedent) is committed,
not pushed, and listed.

**Clear to sign off when** the closing `where-was-i.py --sweep` (step 4) shows no `ACTION` line
except repos listed under "Still open" with their reason, no background job is still writing,
`.errors.log` is empty or its entries are reported, and every repo touched today has a STATUS entry
dated today with a concrete first `## Next` item, and every `card-check` gap is fixed. Questions
only Eric can answer (a receiver nobody named, a decision recorded under `## Open questions`) do
not block: `/startup` shows them tomorrow; list them under "Still open" and say "Clear to sign off".
Anything short of that: "Not clear", naming the one thing blocking.

If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and
note it. A risky fix goes under "Still open".

## Step 1 — Sweep

- **Repo sweep:** `python3 ~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py --sweep` (~4 s). It checks every git
  repo under `DEV/` (two levels) and the three config repos, and prints one line per repo needing
  attention; exit 1 means at least one `ACTION`. Another session, harness or machine may have left
  that work; name each such repo in the report. Flags:
  - `DIRTY`, `UNPUSHED`, `NO-UPSTREAM`, `BRANCH-AHEAD:<b>`, `BRANCH-UNPUSHED:<b>` (a local branch
    holding commits on no remote), `WORKTREE-DIRTY:<path>`: work not on GitHub. Step 4 pushes it.
  - `NOT-A-REPO`: a `.git` folder git cannot use, so the folder's work is tracked nowhere. List it;
    repair is project work, not closeout. It blocks only if this session wrote files there.
  - Info, never blocking: `STASH:<n>` (list it; leave the stash alone), `NO-REMOTE`, `DETACHED`
    (a pinned checkout), `LIVE` (session files the hooks rewrite every turn; the daily backup
    pushes them).
- **Background jobs** still running (shells, agents, workflows): wait for each to finish, or name
  it as the blocker. A job that writes after the push leaves work unpushed.
- **Registry drift:** `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py crosswalk` (`portfolio_json` is
  in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.macos.json`). It only reports. List every item under "Still
  open", any folder created this session first (a project started without a row). Fixing waits
  for a project session. `drive_unreachable` means the Drive checks never ran: say so.
- **7-day rule:** `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py seven-day --apply`. Name every
  project it paused, and any on its last two days, under "Still open" with what it needs (a
  receiver, a first step).
- Unfinished tasks from this session (TaskList), and anything promised to Eric this session and
  not delivered.

## Step 2 — Memory

Memory capture failing silently is Eric's top recurring worry; this step runs every time.

- **`~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log`:** surface every entry, fix the hook issue if
  obvious, then archive and clear it as in claude-stack-doctor's `FIXES.md` → Memory pipeline
  (append to `.errors-ledger.log`, then `cp /dev/null`). The file is tracked in `global-memory`,
  so this happens before step 4's push.
- **Today's transcript** `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` exists and changed within
  the last few hours.
- **New durable decision or active thread:** update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md`
  (2,500-char cap; consolidate first) or write a Tier A memory with the `memory-write` skill.
- **Tier A stays on this machine** (its slug is built from the absolute path, which differs per
  machine). Every durable, project-scoped Tier A fact written today also goes into the repo:
  `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reason, the dated
  handoff for detail.

## Step 3 — STATUS, handoff, cards

**Handoff**, when real work happened (not just Q&A): `<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md`;
workspace or system work with no single repo goes to `~/DEV/docs/handoffs/`
(`~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` is read-only history). Plain markdown that Codex,
Antigravity or a fresh Claude session can resume from:
- what was worked on and why
- decisions made, with the reasoning that would be lost
- exact paths of every file created or modified
- next actions, most important first
- anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

**`docs/STATUS.md`, in every repo touched, every time.** The next session reads it first, on
either machine, in any harness. Rewrite these sections in place, short:
- `## Current state`: two to five lines on where things stand today.
- `## Next`: most important first. Item 1 is one concrete action (a command to run or a file to
  open); `~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py` shows it to Eric the next morning.
- `## Open questions`: each decision waiting on Eric as its own top-level bullet, the question and
  enough context to answer it without opening another file. `/startup` lists this section across
  repos, so write the question itself, never a pointer. Mark answered items `ANSWERED <date>: …`
  or strike them (`~~…~~`). Leave the section empty when nothing waits.
- `## Gotchas`: anything that will bite the next session.

Over 20 KB, or more than 15 dated entries under `## Current state`: first move entries older than
14 days and finished `## Next` items, verbatim, to the end of
`docs/handoffs/STATUS-archive-<YYYY>-Q<n>.md`. The archive is a search root; entries move, they
are never deleted.

Then:
1. `python ~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py --decisions --days 1` prints what tomorrow's
   `/startup` shows as "Decisions waiting on you". Every decision left open today appears there as
   a readable question; fix the repo's `## Open questions` until it does.
2. `python <dir of portfolio_json>/landed.py scan --days 1` (~1 min), then
   `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py card-check`. Fix every gap with
   [`CARDS.md`](CARDS.md), then re-run `card-check`.
3. `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh`: copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into
   `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/` (gitignored, indexed by memsearch). One line of output.
4. **Deliverables:** a finished file made for someone else today (PDF, deck, report, sheet) gets a
   copy at `~/DEV/_DRIVE/03_REPORTS/YYYY-MM-DD_<Sport>_<Topic>_<Audience>.<ext>`. The repo keeps
   the source.

## Step 4 — Commit and push

- **Registry edits first, alone.** In project-triage, if `git status --porcelain portfolio.json`
  shows a change, commit that file alone as `data: board edits <YYYY-MM-DD>`. The board's "N
  unpushed registry edits" counts these; folded into another commit, they become a JSON merge
  conflict when the other machine edits too.
- **Before staging,** read the files about to be added (`git status --porcelain`). Anything the
  `BLOCKED` list in `~/.claude/hooks/session-autopush.js` names (`.env`, keys, credentials,
  secrets, token files, databases, DEXA) or over 50 MB stays out: add it to `.gitignore`, or leave
  it unstaged and list it. Health data never reaches GitHub.
- Every repo in scope: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase`, push. On
  a merge conflict follow `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (the one home for conflict steps), push, and list the
  file under "Still open". A side branch the sweep flagged: `git push -u origin <branch>`.
- `~/.claude/mods` changed this session: `bash ~/.claude/mods/mods-sync.sh`; list any invalid mod.
- **`global-memory` is pushed every time,** even on a light session: it is the only repo that
  carries memory to the other machine, and the nightly backup is too late for a same-day switch.
- Nothing to commit: one line, move on.
- **Prove it:** re-run `python3 ~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py --sweep`. Every `ACTION` line left
  is either fixed now or goes under "Still open" with its reason. A push that hangs is usually a
  credential prompt: look for `git credential-osxkeychain get` in `ps`; fix and retry once, as
  `~/.claude/projects/-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory/project_brew-git-keychain-hang.md` says.
  Still hanging: "Not clear", that repo is the blocker.

## Step 5 — Verdict

`python <dir of portfolio_json>/landed.py show --days 1` lists every file that landed today (git in
every DEV repo, file times on Drive and in the vault), so the report names every created or
modified file with its full path. The ledger lives in `~/.claude/global-memory/landed/` and was
pushed in step 4.

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what> / skipped: <what> (Cowork)
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Registry drift:** <N items, or "none">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.

**Landed:** <landed.py show output, grouped by project>
**Cards:** <card-check output after the step 3 fixes>
```

The block above the verdict line fits on one screen: Eric is leaving. Landed and Cards come last
because the next session picks up from them; trim both to projects with work today, keeping every
card that still has a gap.

# Skill mechanics

The skill-specific branch of [`writing-for-agents`](SKILL.md): what changes when the document is a skill (frontmatter, the invocation choice, and router skills). Everything else about writing it is the universal reference in `SKILL.md`.

## Invocation

Two choices, trading the two loads:

- A **model-invoked** skill keeps a `description`, so the agent can fire it autonomously, and other skills can reach it. You can still type its name: model-invocation always _includes_ user reach; a description only ever adds agent discovery, never removes the human's. The description is the skill's top-level context pointer, forced to stay loaded at all times: permanent context load in exchange for discoverability. A model-invoked skill whose content is all reference is also one home for shared reference: another skill can invoke it, so reference needed by several skills lives in one place. Mechanics: omit `disable-model-invocation`, and write a model-facing description carrying the trigger branches (the pointer-writing rules in `SKILL.md` apply in full).
- A **user-invoked** skill strips the description from the agent's reach: only the human typing its name can invoke it, and no other skill can. Zero context load, but it spends cognitive load: you are the index that must remember it exists. Mechanics: set `disable-model-invocation: true`; the `description` becomes human-facing: a one-line summary, trigger lists stripped.

Pick model-invocation only when the agent must reach the skill on its own, or another skill must. If it only ever fires by hand, make it user-invoked and pay no context load.

Shared reference that two user-invoked skills both need can live in neither: with no descriptions, neither can fire the other. Push it to a plain file outside the skill system: external reference any skill can point at.

## Splitting by invocation

The invocation cut of splitting (the sequence cut lives in `SKILL.md`): split off a model-invoked skill when you have a distinct leading word that should trigger it on its own (a trigger word you actually use in your prompts), or another skill must reach it. You pay context load for the new always-loaded description, so that independent reach has to be worth it.

## Router skills

When user-invoked skills multiply past what you can remember, that piled-up cognitive load is cured by a **router skill**: one user-invoked skill that names the others and when to reach for each, so the human has one skill to remember instead of many. It can only hint, never fire them: user-invoked skills have no description, so nothing but the human can reach them.
